note: Rules for the beat-driven style sheet (pop, hip-hop, trap, funk, house). Hand-written from general knowledge of these styles, not taken from a book and not produced by NDI: the four parsed books stop in 1900. Each rule is sent only when the piece uses the beat-driven sheet.

rules.text: Match the tempo to the groove: lo-fi 70 to 90 BPM, boom-bap 82 to 96, funk 95 to 115, house 118 to 128, trap 130 to 150 felt in half time.
Beat-driven music lives in 4/4; choose another meter only when the prompt asks for something lopsided.
Minor and Dorian suit most hip-hop, trap and house; Dorian and Mixolydian suit funk; pop works in major or minor. Phrygian darkens trap.
Keep the harmony to a loop of two to four chords: sevenths and ninths for funk and soul-leaning grooves, bare minor triads or suspended chords for trap.
A beat needs a kick, a snare, hats and a bass before anything else: drum kit and sub bass (or an 808 kick) come first, then one or two melodic colours, each with a clear job.
Build in blocks of four or eight bars: intro, verse-like section, hook, breakdown, final hook. A recurring hook suits a beat better than one long arc.
Energy comes from adding and removing layers, not from getting louder: plan a breakdown that strips back to pad and motif before the biggest section.
The drop is the climax: the beat thins or stops for a bar, then kick and bass return together at full weight.
Bring the hook back often: in loop music the listener wants the same idea again, in a fuller or a barer setting.
Start with a partial texture (motif and pad, or drums alone) and let the full beat arrive after four or eight bars.
A hook is short: three to five notes, a strong rhythm, mostly steps and repeated notes, ending where it can loop straight back to its start.
Rhythm makes a hook memorable more than pitch does: prefer a syncopated or short-short-long cell, and leave space after it.
Repeated notes are a strength in a hook, not a weakness: a chant on one or two pitches can carry a whole beat.
Loop the motif: leaving it intact for several phrases is right. When it changes, change one thing: an octave, the last note, a displaced start.
Keep a loop alive with call and response between two sounds: the motif asks, another instrument answers in the gap.
Change chords once a bar or once every two bars; two chords alternating are enough for a whole section.
End phrases unresolved so the loop turns over; save the resolved ending for the last phrase.
Fragment the motif during a build, then state it whole at the drop.
Keep pad voicings still: hold the common tones and move the others by step, so the chord change is felt in the bass.
Let the bass take the root: inversions weaken a groove's low end. A pedal bass under changing chords builds tension before a drop.
Kick and bass are one instrument: the bass hits with the kick in trap and boom-bap, pumps in eighths under a four-on-the-floor kick, and plays a syncopated figure in funk.
Snare on beats two and four is the backbone of pop, funk, house and boom-bap; trap moves it to beat three for a half-time feel.
Hi-hats set the energy: eighths for a relaxed section, sixteenths to push, rolls only as punctuation at the end of a bar.
Raise drum intensity through a section rather than starting at the top; drop the drums out for a bar or a whole phrase to make their return hit.
Keep the low register for the kick and one bass sound: no low strings, low piano or pedal notes under a sub bass.
Put the hook on a short bright sound (pluck, piano, vibraphone) in the middle register, above the pad and well clear of the bass.
Use the low-pass filter as the arrangement: closed for intros and breakdowns, opening through a build, fully open at the drop.
Sidechain pump belongs with a four-on-the-floor or pop kick under a sustained pad or bass; leave it off in sparse boom-bap.
Keep reverb short and the mix dry and punchy; save long reverb and delay for the breakdown and for single notes left hanging.
A little saturation adds weight to drums and 808 bass; add more as the energy rises.
Before a drop, take something away: mute the kick for the last bar, close the filter, or stop everything for a beat.
Do not thicken a beat with doublings: one sound per job. Add or remove whole layers instead.
Trap: 808 bass notes are long and few, hats run in sixteenths with rolls, and the melody is sparse, dark and repetitive.
Funk: every part is percussion. Keep notes short, leave gaps, and let the parts interlock so that no two hit all the same sixteenths.
House: once the kick is in it never stops, except in the breakdown; open hats off the beat and a pumping bass carry the drive.
Boom-bap: drums loud and swung, bass simple and round, one looped motif on a warm colour such as piano or vibraphone.
Judge a loop by its groove and its hook: prefer the draft whose rhythm is strongest and whose notes are fewest.
In loop music sameness is not a fault: reject a phrase for drifting from the hook, never for repeating it.
End a beat by taking layers away until only the motif or the pad is left, or stop dead on a downbeat; a slow ritardando does not belong.
While holding, keep the pad sounding and move the filter: a beat can sit on one chord for a long time.
The chorus is the fullest section: every layer in, the hook on top, the widest and brightest mix. Keep verses leaner so the chorus has somewhere to go.
Each chorus should top the one before: add a layer, a doubling or an octave. The last chorus is the biggest moment of the song.
Set up a chorus or a drop by taking something away just before it: drop the drums or bass for the last bar, so their return is felt.
A bridge or breakdown gives the ear something else: thin the beat, change the chords or the melody, so the last chorus lands fresh.
In a verse keep the texture lean: drums, bass and one more layer, with the hook held back or only hinted at.
A chorus is the same music each time it returns; by the second one the listener should be able to sing along.
